n: This verse follows the usual formula for a king's reign, but the Hebrew numbers seem damaged — literally “Saul was a year old.” Translators and scholars still debate the original figures.

f.g: The Hebrew reads “Saul was … years old when he began to reign, and he reigned … two years,” with numbers apparently lost in copying.

n: Saul forms a standing army of three thousand, keeping two thousand with himself near Michmash and Bethel and placing one thousand under his son Jonathan at Gibeah.

f.g: Saul's eldest son; his name means “the LORD has given.”
A town on a ridge north of a steep valley, facing Geba across the pass.

n: Jonathan attacks a Philistine outpost at Geba, essentially declaring war. Saul sounds the trumpet across the land to rally the Israelites.

f.g: Possibly a military post, or a governor's pillar marking Philistine control.
A ram's horn (shofar) used to call people to battle.

n: News spreads that Saul has struck the Philistines and that Israel is now hated by them. The people gather to Saul at Gilgal.

f.g: became a stench, hated

n: The Philistines respond with an enormous army, including many chariots, and camp at Michmash. Israel is badly outmatched.

f.g: Some ancient versions read three thousand, which fits better with six thousand horsemen.
“House of wickedness,” a place near Bethel.

n: Seeing the danger, many Israelites panic and hide in caves, thickets, rocks, tombs, and pits.

f.g: in a tight spot, in serious trouble

n: Some even flee across the Jordan. Saul remains at Gilgal, but his remaining troops are trembling with fear.

f.g: Israelite territories east of the Jordan.

n: Saul waits the seven days Samuel had appointed, but Samuel has not arrived, and Saul's army is deserting him. The pressure on Saul is intense.

f.w: the set time that Samuel had appointed

n: Unwilling to wait any longer, Saul offers the burnt offering himself instead of waiting for the Lord's prophet.

f.g: Saul took on a sacred duty Samuel was to perform.

n: Just as Saul finishes, Samuel arrives. Saul goes out to greet him as if nothing were wrong.

f.g: greet him

n: Samuel asks, “What have you done?” Saul makes excuses: the army was scattering, Samuel was late, and the Philistines were gathering.
Saul says he feared attack before seeking the Lord's favor, so he “forced himself” to offer the sacrifice. He sounds reluctant but still chose fear over obedience.

f.g: sought the Lord's favor
I felt compelled

n: Samuel declares that Saul acted foolishly by disobeying God's command. Had he obeyed, the Lord would have established his dynasty permanently.
Now Saul's dynasty will not last. The Lord has already found “a man after his own heart” — David — to lead His people.

f.w: a man after his own heart

f.g: leader, ruler (Hebrew nagid)

n: Samuel leaves for Gibeah. Saul counts his remaining troops: only about six hundred men are left from his three thousand.
Saul and Jonathan hold Gibeah with their small force, while the Philistines camp across the valley at Michmash.
The Philistines send out three raiding parties to plunder the countryside. The first heads north toward Ophrah.

f.g: raiders, plunderers

n: The second goes west toward Beth-horon, and the third east toward the wilderness. Israel's land is open to raids in every direction.
The Philistines had a monopoly on metalworking and allowed no blacksmiths in Israel, to keep the Israelites from making iron weapons.

f.g: blacksmith, metalworker

n: Israelites had to go to the Philistines just to sharpen their farm tools — an economic and military stranglehold.

f.g: plowshare, the blade of a plow
Another farming tool, possibly a mattock or axe.
a digging tool like a pickaxe

n: The Philistines charged fees for sharpening tools. The Hebrew here includes the word pim, which archaeologists have found on weights equal to about two-thirds of a shekel — the price charged.

f.g: The Hebrew is pim, a weight (about two-thirds of a shekel) — the price for sharpening.
pointed sticks for driving oxen

n: So when war came, only Saul and Jonathan had swords or spears. Israel would have to rely on the Lord rather than on weapons.
The Philistines move a detachment to guard the pass at Michmash, setting up the dramatic events of the next chapter.

f.g: A steep ravine between Geba and Michmash.
